hints: Start from what you know sucrose is made of - it is a disaccharide split into two monomers in Fig. 5.1, one is glucose in the form alpha-glucose-1-phosphate, so what must the other monomer be?
walkthrough:
Recall What Sucrose Is Made From**
Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose joined to fructose. In Fig. 5.1 the reaction splits sucrose using inorganic phosphate, so the two products must be those two monomers in modified form.

Match The Products**
One product is shown as alpha-glucose-1-phosphate, which is the glucose half. That leaves X as the other half, which is the reducing sugar fructose.

hints: Think about what happens first when sucrose and phosphate meet the enzyme - where do they fit and what complex is formed?
Think about the energy barrier that normally makes the reaction slow, and how holding reactants close together changes that barrier.
walkthrough:
Forming The Enzyme-Substrate Complex**
Sucrose and phosphate fit into the active site of sucrose phosphorylase. The active site has a shape and chemistry complementary to them, so an enzyme-substrate complex forms and the reactants are held close together in the correct orientation.

Providing An Easier Route**
By holding substrates together and stressing key bonds, the enzyme provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. That means a much larger proportion of molecules have enough energy to react at any moment, so rate increases greatly.
Final answer: substrate(s) bind to active site to form enzyme-substrate complex, holding reactants close together; lowers activation energy so more molecules react per unit time.

hints: Compare the peaks in Fig. 5.3 first - read off the temperature of maximum 100% activity for the free enzyme circles and for the immobilised enzyme crosses.
Look at the shape of the curves in Fig. 5.2 - which enzyme keeps activity high over a wider pH range, and what happens at pH 4.5 to 5.5?
Link high temperature to the industrial clue about microorganisms - which enzyme is still very active above $68^{\circ}C$ up to $80^{\circ}C$?
Balance the argument - where is the free enzyme actually better, and what cost or practical points favour each form for industry?
walkthrough:
Read The Temperature Optima From Fig. 5.3**
The free enzyme peaks at 100% activity around $56^{\circ}C$ to $59^{\circ}C$, while the immobilised enzyme peaks much higher at around $74^{\circ}C$ to $76^{\circ}C$. That is about a $17^{\circ}C$ higher optimum for the immobilised form.

Compare Stability At High Temperature And pH**
Above about $68^{\circ}C$ the free enzyme falls steeply to about $67$% at $70^{\circ}C$, while the immobilised enzyme is still rising to $90$% to $100$%. In Fig. 5.2 the immobilised enzyme also keeps high activity over a broader pH range, for example at pH 4.5 it is about $69$% while free is only about $32$%, and at pH 5.0 it is about $91$% while free is about $51$%. So pH changes have less effect on the immobilised enzyme.

Link To Industrial Needs**
Industry wants high temperature to kill contaminating microorganisms and wants stability. The immobilised enzyme is more thermostable and pH tolerant, plus it has general immobilised advantages: reusable, longer shelf-life, no contamination of product by enzyme and easy separation for continuous processing.

Give The Balanced Case For Free Enzyme**
The free enzyme is not useless. Between about $35^{\circ}C$ to $68^{\circ}C$ it shows higher relative activity than immobilised at the same temperature. Its lower optimum means less heating cost, and around $57^{\circ}C$ is still hot enough to reduce microbial growth. Overall, for very hot, variable conditions immobilised is better, for lower-cost moderate temperature work free is better.

Final answer: Immobilised better for high-temperature, variable pH industry: optimum temp ~$75^{\circ}C$ vs ~$57^{\circ}C$ for free; more active above $68^{\circ}C$ and more stable over wider pH range; reusable with longer shelf-life and no product contamination. Free enzyme has higher activity between ~$35^{\circ}C$ to $68^{\circ}C$ and lower optimum so cheaper to heat, still high enough to reduce microbes.
